speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Hey, this is Carlos, CEO at Product School and your host on The Product Podcast. My guest today is Faisal Masud, SVP and President of HP Digital Services, which is HP's software business. His path there is odd in the best way: six years at Amazon, then eBay, Groupon, CTO at Staples, then COO at Wing, Alphabet's drone-delivery moonshot, then CEO of Fabric. Now he runs software inside a company most people still think of as printers, and his platform tells customers to buy less hardware. Things we'll cover in this episode: the irony of the AI manifesto and the slop it produced; AI is part of your strategy, it cannot be the strategy; selling a product that tells HP customers to buy fewer HP machines; outcome-based pricing when you have fewer human seats to charge for; and why the middle-management layer is the one AI actually removes. Let's get into it. Welcome to The Product Podcast, Faisal.

speaker: Faisal Masud
text: Nice to meet you. Understanding the Title, and Why HP Built a Software Business

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Your title is very complicated, so you have to help me here. It says President and SVP of HP Digital Services.

speaker: Faisal Masud
text: That's right. I didn't create the title, but it's the internal title for, basically, running all of HP's commercial software business. So the digital part is essentially anything to do with software that we sell into our enterprises and channel partners.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: That's kind of unique to HP. The first thing someone thinks of with HP is hardware, printers, right? So what was the rationale behind expanding into software as a service?

speaker: Faisal Masud
text: Back when I joined, around that time they were forming an organization that later became Digital Services. It was primarily set up to be exactly that: a bit of a deviation away from the hardware, the separation on purpose, so it could be a standalone operating unit that builds software to support the hardware business. The reason we did it is that it's very hard to just run a purely analog hardware business. You have to have the data around the hardware, and the thesis I've been building with the team has been exactly that: collect telemetry from what we serve our customers with, and then turn those insights back into serving our customers. From E-commerce and Drones to SaaS

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: I was looking at your background. You worked at Amazon, eBay, Google, but the drone-delivery business, Wing, was also really cool. So for someone who comes mostly from e-commerce, with a stint in drone delivery, how did you end up in SaaS?

speaker: Faisal Masud
text: I ended up in SaaS completely by accident, because the early days of this started around my time at Fabric. After I left Alphabet and Wing, I joined some ex-colleagues from Staples and eBay who had started a company called Fabric, and I joined as CEO. At that time we were very, very early, still doing our seed round, so I got involved pretty early in the product. The interesting part is we had built something similar at Staples for our e-commerce platform, where we were trying to transition away from the legacy IBM WebSphere. So this became a platform we could serve to everybody that wasn't Amazon, that didn't have all the capabilities Amazon had. That's where my journey into SaaS started. Most of our selling was founder-led selling for SaaS. I took that company from seed to Series C, stayed on the board for a bit soon thereafter, and then joined here. The Irony of the AI Manifesto and the Slop It Produced

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: I was going down the rabbit hole on your X profile, and I found a couple of interesting tweets I want to bring up. One was a response to Tobi, co-founder of Shopify. He's all over the place again because he's talking about the AI slop grenade, but he was also the originator of the CEO AI manifesto encouraging people to use AI. And it seems like now people are using AI in ways that aren't very great. So what's your take on that?

speaker: Faisal Masud
text: My take, and I wrote about this, is that the FOMO is off the charts. Two years ago it was completely off the charts, and now it's settling down a bit with all the tokens spent. But I always find it's good to be an early adopter, and it's also good to have some data around the adoption, versus just going all-in. The response you're referring to might have been one around the slop grenades he's talking about. The irony I found was: on one hand, we're encouraging everybody that AI will replace every job, don't come to a meeting if you haven't figured it out with AI, and encouraging that as much as possible. And then, on the other hand, talking about how it's just slop central and that's what's happening. With the introduction of AI at work, for those adopting it, it's becoming hard to understand what's actually written by a human versus pure slop. I find it ironic that you can't encourage an organization to go all-in, which is what they did, with no guardrails around it, and then, on the other hand, have a problem with the massive amounts of slop in your organization. You have to pick your lane. Getting Through the Slop to Quality

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Maybe coming from a startup myself, I also encourage my team to go all-in with AI. And of course, we have to get through slop. I actually had to get through slop in many ways. But I thought of that as a necessary step in order to achieve quality. I wonder if you've found ways to achieve quality without getting through the nitty-gritty of some slop along the way?

speaker: Faisal Masud
text: AI has a very dominant position in what we do at our enterprise, and even outside a startup environment, AI is really good at the inform and consult part of the equation: getting information so you can consult with it. But what it can't be is completely copy-paste. That's where things get difficult, because human judgment is going to become really important here. If you lack ideas and you're relying heavily on AI for everything, you're not really going to be that important. Nassim Taleb recently tweeted this. I don't know if you follow him, but he said something like, those with high IQ and no original ideas are going to find it very hard in the world of AI. And I tend to agree. You have to be creative at the same time as utilizing AI along the way. So I think you did the right thing, and you probably expected the slop to go up and at some point come back down. I'm still waiting for the come-back-down part.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: That's true. It's also easy to give up, or to just stay in that slop stage and not push through enough. That's what I found is a lack of, for most of the clients we work with. They're doing all the right things on paper: they send the AI manifesto, they buy the tools, they create some metrics around adoption. But clearly that's not enough.

speaker: Faisal Masud
text: I've seen enough tools now flooding the market: knowledge graph this, integrated into all your collaboration tools, getting alerts and alarms through bots powered by the litany of providers. In some cases they're adding more work. They're actually introducing more work into your daily workflow, not deducting it. So where I have a challenge is: AI is not your strategy. It's part of your strategy. It's going to help with your strategy. It cannot become the strategy, because then you've got a problem. It's a tool in the toolkit. It's not going to be the be-all and end-all. Leveraging it in the best way possible while utilizing human judgment, that's where the real impact is. The AI Layer Being Built on Top of SaaS

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: I want to get your take on this AI layer we're seeing built on top of a lot of SaaS. You come from e-commerce, so you've seen how, now, anyone can throw agents at SaaS to go do things. I've been obsessed with some of these new consumer agents for personal work. So how do you think about that as an actual tool for employee productivity?

speaker: Faisal Masud
text: We're on frontier with OpenAI, and it's fairly integrated here at HP with the latest models. To answer your question on some of these consumer agents, you're very courageous to use one, in the sense that you give it all your logins, passwords, and so on. I feel like privacy and security are going to become a big obstacle along the way. It's not going to be trivial to just hand over all your credentials to one bot that's going to go do what it needs to do. People might be very selective about what they use it for. You saw Amazon decline to work with some of these agents, just like the decline with Perplexity. I don't know where I stand on that, because I feel like Amazon's moat is Prime, and customers will continue to go to Amazon because of Prime. They don't need those agents, not today, at least. When it comes to the enterprise, I think Microsoft has done a pretty decent job at this point. The early days were a bit rockier, but with Copilot, the integration of Copilot, and their soon-to-come coworker and Claude for enterprise, I think it's a good product for those who want the capabilities AI can provide alongside their work. The most integrated product right now is probably Microsoft. I don't find that same level of native capabilities out of Google Workspace, at least I haven't seen it there, it's not as integrated. Whereas if you look at Microsoft, Copilot has actually made a lot of gains. HP's Own AI Strategy: Internal Workflows First

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: So where do you play in this arena? You're running the SaaS portfolio for HP, and now you have all of these agent opportunities along the way. So what's your strategy?

speaker: Faisal Masud
text: Our strategy is for internal workflows. I'm not running IT for the organizations I sell into; I sell into IT leaders. But for our internal organization, the product managers are pushed very hard: what can be done through AI should be done through AI, and what needs a human in the loop, you do that. So the PMs use all the tools available, whether it's the early days of ChatGPT down to Claude now, and wherever they can use tools, they do all that work, from ideation to PRD and beyond. A lot of that is getting heavily compressed. Even early demo videos are so easy now. Everything is just so much easier now, until you need to go to production. That's a whole different ballgame. What we do internally is try to make sure we can leverage as much of the out-of-the-box capabilities Microsoft provides in every facet possible, and then internally accelerate our overall cycle time for getting from ideation all the way to deploying features to the market. Our developers use Codex, Claude Code, and the PMs are all pretty heavy users of AI as well. Pushing Through Enterprise Bureaucracy

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: To what extent, though? In the startup world there's no backup plan, so everybody is forced to move as fast as possible, while in a larger enterprise you can still find ways to slow down. You come from a massive company. Your company is more of a spin-off here, but still it's not small. So how do you push through bureaucracy and other barriers to make sure your PMs can move as fast as possible?

speaker: Faisal Masud
text: Large organizations are about relationships. As much as there's friction to get approvals for certain tools or capabilities, which could be exposure for the organization, you have to build the internal relationships to bring people with you. Early on, back when I joined, Figma was pretty popular, but it wasn't really being utilized much internally. I pushed very hard to make sure that whatever out-of-the-box capabilities Figma provided, we were using for all our design. That's now obviously moved forward to pretty much being able to do everything with the toolset you have internally. I've not seen a ton of challenges outside of the fact that, when you're using a lot of these products, the tokens run out fairly quickly and the budgets are challenging. So that's where it comes down to: where's the ROI for all of this? Because if you can't see the ROI on the amount of money you're spending on those tokens, you have to be able to do the math and be okay with it. When it comes to friction internally, I'd say we haven't faced the level of friction I would assume from a large enterprise like ourselves in utilizing the tools available. Change Has to Come From the Top

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: One thing I can imagine from the outside is that a lot of these initiatives at this level have to happen from the very top. Having a leader who is not just talking the talk but walking the walk is necessary. I've seen this so many times with some of our clients: they want to be more AI-native, but they're not really committing to the pain it takes to make it happen. You need someone fighting from the very top, otherwise AI becomes a cute initiative for some people to raise a trophy and say, "I checked my box."

speaker: Faisal Masud
text: I can tell you there was a lot of blood, sweat, and tears going into building the original thesis for Workforce Experience. We're in a business where our platform provides insights on our customers' total surface area: their hardware, software, OS, network, and so on. But at the same time, we also encourage buying less, which is counterproductive to a hardware business, right? So why do we do that? Because ultimately we exist because we want to make that employee experience absolutely world-class. And you can't make a world-class employee experience if you've got a bias in the process. From the top, you have to make sure that bias is removed, and your central focus, your grounding principle, is: how do I improve the experience for the people I'm selling this into? For that, you have to make some trade-offs. To your point, it wasn't easy to convince everybody, but it's less about convincing everyone. It's really important to convince yourself first: Will this work? How relevant is it? Will it have ROI for the people you're selling it into? Is there product-market fit? Is this a plug product, or are you selling it into these people? You have to go through all these questions. Once we found we had PMF, it was all roads leading to "let's go build this faster." Go-to-Market: Selling the Solution, Not the Hardware

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: As you talk about product-market fit, I want to know your go-to-market motion. How much are you leveraging your existing HP relationships to introduce your product, versus going to market directly?

speaker: Faisal Masud
text: We do both. One big friction point early on, although it didn't really become an issue, was when I started pitching Workforce Experience as not a point solution, which we used to have back in the day. Point solutions are interesting, but they're not that relevant to the economic buyer long-term. When you're pitching a platform, the platform has to be completely agnostic of your own stuff that's involved in it. So we went device-agnostic and OS-agnostic. We didn't care if the fleets we were selling into were competitors' brands or a completely different OS. Our principled approach was: we don't care what hardware you're running, we want to make sure we can help you run that environment better. Once you have those very specific principles outlined on why you're doing that, and people are on board, it becomes a lot easier to move forward. On how we do the go-to-market: we rely heavily on our existing go-to-market rails. As a very large hardware seller, an OEM, we are constantly in conversations where our account reps are dealing with customers who are buying competitor product. In the past, HP used to sell third-party software. We don't do that anymore. All the IP we've built, we're selling as our own software. So the transition was basically: we're not going to do that anymore, we're going to sell our own home-built, owned-IP product. In those conversations, what's evolved now is that instead of selling hardware, we're selling the solution: what problem are you trying to solve? Our go-to-market relies heavily on CIOs and RFPs coming in with explanations around "we're trying to solve this problem," and Workforce Experience fits into that, versus selling the software with the hardware, which just doesn't scale. How Close Are You to the Outcome?

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: The million-dollar question for a lot of the CIOs being pitched software, hardware, hybrid solutions is: how close are you to the outcome, versus just telling me that with this new software my employees are going to increase productivity by X percent?

speaker: Faisal Masud
text: We're very clear on that, because when we started dogfooding the product inside HP, it wasn't a low bar. It was a high bar to convince our own IT teams to use it. We had 80,000 devices and hundreds, if not thousands, of pieces of software running in these environments. We had to convince our internal teams that this is the path forward and it will help them manage HP's IT environment better. Not until we crossed that threshold and accomplished some success there did we even go to market. So we had a very long alpha, a pretty long beta, then an extended release. We didn't go GA for a long time, and at every stage we had 15 to 20 to 100 partners alongside us looking at the ROI of what we deliver. An example: we're not walking into our customers' offices saying, "buy this and we'll promise you the world and nothing will happen on the other side." We're actually telling them their ticket volume will go down by 30 to 40%, because Workforce Experience will tackle all those tickets behind the scenes. That's pure ROI, because all those tickets are managed by desk-side support. One ticket is, I don't know, six, ten, twenty dollars, whatever it takes to resolve, and it's a headache for the employee. Second, we have a feature called Smart Refresh, which evaluates all your fleet and says what you should not be buying. In the IT industry, what ends up happening is hardware is bought on 3-to-4-year cycles, in a really monolithic process: "it's done this way, so that's the way we'll do it again, let's go buy 100,000 machines." We're breaking that mold and saying, actually, no, you shouldn't be buying 100,000 machines. You should be buying 55,000 machines, upgrade these, and Workforce Experience can manage all the others in a perfect configuration, so you can extend the life of your machine. That comes at a very low cost to them, because we can manage all of it. But think about that for a second: nobody else is doing that.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: As an executive myself, that's what I need to hear. How is this solution going to make me more money, or save me some cost? Everything in between is kind of unclear.

speaker: Faisal Masud
text: If we can't provide that return on their investment, we shouldn't exist. It's as simple as that. The right to be in the room is only allowed until we can demonstrate the performance. We've had partners come back and tell us that not only has their ticket volume gone down, their mean average time to resolve tickets has gone down by 30%. So what used to take six or seven days is now taking two or three days. Those are the types of things we love hearing. We saw that when folks are refreshing their fleets, they're spending 20, 30 million, and they're spending 25 to 30% less. In the end, that's all cash. That's all cash leaving their enterprise. If Workforce Experience can help you with that, isn't that what you want? You want to reduce costs, be more secure, and have higher velocity in your IT environment. What AI Does to the Management Layer

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: You have a front-row seat to workforce transformation. You're seeing companies go up and down in headcount, especially now with AI. So I'm really curious: what do you think is going to happen in the midterm due to the AI impact on business?

speaker: Faisal Masud
text: I mentioned this in a previous podcast, about the layers. What AI is demonstrably doing immediately is that those additional layers of management are just not that necessary anymore. Longer-term, because a lot of that monitoring, management, data collection, and aggregation of information can be done by individuals, if you have to rely on a manager reporting to a manager reporting to a director, I'm not sure all those layers scale long-term with AI, because AI can do a lot of that work. That's one. Second, we're seeing a lot of requests, and we've built a new alpha in our labs, a product called AI Command Center. So when you buy Workforce Experience in the future, there's a capability that comes with our elite package that will look at your entire landscape of employees and their AI adoption, usage, and yield. We can actually help you predict and manage not just your budgeting, but also how your employees are adopting all the technology you're releasing to them. That's something we're hearing a lot more about: how can I make sure my employees are more efficient at what they do? The challenge has been that most of these CIOs haven't seen the return from all of these things, and we want to give them a clear, visible line of sight: here are the employees by department, by persona, by usage, using these models. How can you make them more efficient? How can you make sure there's adoption in the right places? That's what people are looking for. Ultimately, to your question, you'll still have people in these organizations, but fundamentally, managers will have to know a lot more than just managing. Who Manages the Fleet of Agents?

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: That's a real challenge right now. In my case, we're deploying a bunch of agents, obsessing over it, really finding ways to use AI instead of a human when we have a problem. But the problem we're creating on the back end is: who's going to manage this fleet of agents? How good are they? When do we actually need a human instead of an agent, or a combination? I still haven't seen a way to easily manage that type of relationship.

speaker: Faisal Masud
text: It's not a trivial one to manage, because, back to your earlier point, agents just talking to agents all day long, I'm not sure. Ultimately, someone has to make a decision. When it's a higher-fidelity decision, there's going to be a human involved, because agents are not going to have responsibility for those. So I could envision a place, in the retail arena for example, where a traditional retailer has a buyer, a planner, and a merchandiser who does all the marketing activity, and they'd all have assistants next to them: an assistant buyer, a planner level one, a site merchandiser level one, with AI. I think those second levels are agents, and those first-level buyers are now not managers. They're actually ICs managing agents. That's the format I see. What is a buyer in e-commerce ultimately doing all day? They're negotiating prices, submitting POs, selecting product, selecting vendors. Those tasks don't seem, in the world of these new AI agents, like they can't be done by AI. So the flip is: where you were a manager, one could foresee that now you're managing the agents. What Fewer Human Seats Means for Pricing

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Back to your current business: how does that impact your pricing model? Traditional SaaS bases pricing on seats, and now you have fewer human seats. So what does that mean for you?

speaker: Faisal Masud
text: Fewer human seats is totally fine by us, because ultimately we're committing to ROI around your spend and your overall ticketing volume: how much are you spending on desk-side support? That's a pretty large expense for large enterprises to manage 24/7. We see a world where those seats could exist and not exist, but move to more of a rev-share model or a cost-reduction model. In the future state, we can imagine a world where you had X number of tickets a year, we commit to this much reduction overall, and based on that, we charge you a fee that's outcome-based. That doesn't seem out of scope, because CIOs are getting smarter about not just paying for dashboards that aren't useful. They're paying for actual outcomes. So I see a clear path: you can be either seat-based with commitments on outcomes, or purely outcome-based. The skin in the game with the outcome-based model makes the equation very equal. It's a win for you and a win for us. The best negotiations in the world are when both parties are winning. If one party is losing, the deal doesn't work out that well long-term; it's really good short-term, you can high-five all day long, but a year later you're churning that customer. So what AI is doing is a bit of a leveling of the playing field: do I need all these pieces of software? What are they doing for me? Are they actually generating ROI? Is there a way to compute that? If there isn't, I don't need it. I kind of like that, because we believe that if it were just a software business not supporting the hardware business, there are so many of those, but we have a unique position.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: We have some extreme examples already in the market, not a lot. A helpdesk platform, for example, just got acquired by Salesforce for $3.6 billion, I believe, and it's all about outcome-based pricing, some number of dollars per ticket resolved. I think the closer we can get our pricing to the outcome of the client, the better for both. It puts extra pressure on the vendor to actually deliver on what they promised, but it's actually a good thing.

speaker: Faisal Masud
text: At some point, why do you want anything inside your IT environment if it's not accretive to the bottom line of what you do? What's the purpose? Just for pretty dashboards? That's meaningless. Staying Close to the Work as an Executive

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: No more dashboards, please. I'm burning dashboards. I don't want more meetings for the sake of meetings. It's been liberating to know I can do a lot of things myself again, like when we were much smaller. It's huge. So I'm curious how that applies at the scale you operate at. You're the President of HP Digital Services, but you're still very in tune with what's going on in the market. What are some of the pockets where you still want to feel a bit more like an IC?

speaker: Faisal Masud
text: I feel fairly liberated with AI, because a lot of the long-tail tasks are being managed through AI. I have an agent that runs overnight and looks at what's really important to me, with pre-drafts ready. I'm doing all the stuff you're probably doing, and everybody in a similar job to mine is probably doing. The usage of AI for executives is very different from the usage of AI for ICs. Let's be clear about this: when you're an executive, you've got a support structure around you that eliminates the need for too much AI, because you've got human beings around you. But where you do need AI, it's there. Where I feel more liberated is that I want to spend as much time as possible with customers, and with existing customers versus new customers. That's number one, because I believe existing customers are more important than new customers. They trusted you, they brought you in, and you have to do everything possible to build a repeatable, predictable product that has ROI. Number two, this AI Command Center I talked about, I'm personally involved in architecting what we're building, and I find that so amazing, because I'm able to be in a room with the PMs and the engineering teams tackling issues like: where's that data going to come from? What are we going to do about this? How are we looking at synthetic data versus real data? How are we going to surface this, and what action are customers going to take? I love that part, because it gets your juices going, to really think about what the ultimate goal is and how we get there. Longer-term, for us, selling more hardware is not the answer. It's selling more actual value to the customer. That could come in a SaaS product combined with hardware, or either or, but it ultimately has to be measurable. So I'm spending a lot more time with upcoming product labs and customers.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: It's been awesome to connect with you and learn from your experience at a pretty large organization that's operating in a pretty AI-native way. Thank you for your time.

speaker: Faisal Masud
text: Thank you, and thanks for some great questions.
